common_name: Blue Princess Verbena (Texas Superstar Trailing Verbena)

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Blue Princess is a Texas Superstar release selected for outstanding heat tolerance combined with better cold tolerance than many trailing verbenas, extending its usable range.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Blue Princess is a Texas Superstar-designated trailing verbena selected specifically for reliable performance across the wide swing between brutal summer heat and occasional hard freezes typical of Texas and the Gulf South, blooming in dense, lavender-blue clusters almost continuously from spring through frost. Its vigorous trailing habit makes it well suited to retaining walls, hanging baskets, and the tops of raised beds where it can spill over the edge, and it holds up to humidity better than many older verbena selections, showing good resistance to the powdery mildew that often disfigures verbena in a humid Southern summer. It is drought tolerant once established and benefits from an occasional shearing back by a third to keep growth dense and encourage a fresh flush of bloom.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Lynn's Legacy Cenizo (Texas Superstar Reliable-Blooming Texas Sage)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in extremely well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Lynn's Legacy is a Texas Superstar cenizo selection named for plantsman Lynn Lowrey, chosen for blooming more reliably and over a longer season than typical cenizo, regardless of humidity swings.

directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, lean, alkaline soil; Lynn's Legacy is a Texas Superstar-designated cenizo, discovered by plantsman Lynn Lowrey near Monterrey, Mexico, and selected because it blooms more consistently and for a longer stretch of the growing season than typical Leucophyllum cenizo, which famously flushes into bloom mainly around rain events. It shares the classic silvery, felted foliage that reflects heat and reduces water loss, along with clusters of lavender-purple tubular flowers, but with a more upright, slightly more refined growth habit than the common species. Never overwater, fertilize heavily, or amend the planting hole with organic matter, since excess moisture and rich soil are the most common causes of decline in cenizo. Outstanding for xeric, native, and wildlife gardens across zones 8-11.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Grandma's Yellow Rose (Texas Superstar Found Heirloom Yellow Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Grandma's Yellow is a Texas Superstar 'found' rose — an old, disease-tough garden survivor identified and propagated by Texas rose experts rather than a modern commercial breeding program release.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Grandma's Yellow is a Texas Superstar-designated rose identified and propagated by Texas horticulturists as a tough, disease-resistant 'found' rose — a survivor discovered thriving in an old home landscape long after the original planting was forgotten, a hallmark of genuinely tough antique and found roses well adapted to Southern conditions. It produces deep golden-yellow, repeat-blooming flowers on a vigorous, disease-resistant shrub that needs far less spray intervention than most modern hybrid tea roses to stay healthy through a humid Gulf South growing season. Like other Texas Superstar-designated found roses, it rewards low-input, minimal-spray care once established — light pruning in late winter and routine watering during dry spells are usually all it needs to perform reliably for years.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Texas Gold Columbine (Big Bend Golden Columbine)

planting.note: Direct sow seed in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification and spring germination, or cold-stratify seed for 3-4 weeks at 40F and sow in early spring; Texas Gold is a Texas Superstar selection of a rare Big Bend native columbine with especially large golden flowers and strong heat tolerance.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Texas Gold is a Texas Superstar-designated selection of a rare native columbine found only in a few canyons of Big Bend National Park, producing exceptionally large, long-spurred, bright golden-yellow flowers on sturdy stems from spring into summer. Selected specifically for outstanding heat and drought tolerance compared to typical garden columbines, it holds up notably well through a Texas or Gulf South summer with far less decline than European columbine hybrids. The long nectar spurs make it an excellent hummingbird and sphinx moth plant. Like other columbines it is relatively short-lived as an individual plant but self-sows readily where happy, naturalizing into a persistent colony over a few seasons if seed heads are allowed to mature and drop.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Orange Frost Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Changsha-Satsuma Hybrid Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, ideally against a south-facing wall for extra winter protection; Orange Frost is a Texas Superstar cold-hardy citrus selection, a Changsha tangerine x satsuma hybrid bred to extend in-ground citrus growing further into zone 8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, ideally in a sheltered, south-facing spot near a wall or structure for extra winter warmth; Orange Frost is a Texas Superstar-designated cold-hardy mandarin, a hybrid between Changsha tangerine and satsuma bred to survive colder winters than standard satsuma varieties can tolerate, extending reliable in-ground citrus growing into zone 8 with proper siting and young-tree protection. It produces small, sweet, easy-peel orange fruit with the classic satsuma-type flavor in fall and early winter. Young trees still need frost protection — cover or use string lights on hard-freeze nights for the first several winters — but a well-established, mature tree in a good microclimate can survive cold snaps that would kill less hardy citrus outright. Water deeply and regularly during establishment and fruit development, and avoid heavy fertilizing late in the season, which can push tender new growth vulnerable to frost.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cold-Hardy Citrus for the Gulf South

common_name: Southern Sensation Seedless Grape (Pierce's Disease-Resistant Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in well-drained soil in full sun; Southern Sensation is a joint Texas A&M / University of Arkansas release, a Texas Superstar seedless table grape with proven long-term resistance to Pierce's disease, the bacterial disease that limits standard table grapes across the humid South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Southern Sensation is a Texas Superstar-designated table grape, a joint release from Texas A&M and University of Arkansas breeding programs, bred to combine yellow, thin-skinned, seedless fruit with strong flavor and years of demonstrated resistance to Pierce's disease — the bacterial disease spread by sharpshooter insects that kills most European-type table grape varieties within a few years across the humid South and has long limited backyard grape growing in Texas and the Gulf region. It has outperformed standard seedless varieties like Flame Seedless in regional trials specifically for disease survival and fruit quality in southern conditions. Prune to a permanent cordon system in late winter, and thin crowded fruit clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation, which helps reduce fungal disease pressure in humid weather.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program
University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Grape Breeding Program
